text:
Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swan. Today, important consumer advice for men heading for a prostate
biopsy. Barbaric is what one urologist calls the commonest technique for doing
this. Keep your legs crossed till then.

Canada's first female aboriginal psychiatrist is on the program, Canadian First
Nations, like ours, experienced stolen generations, in their case through
residential schools. But unlike Australia, Canada has had a Truth and
Reconciliation Commission. Find out more later.

How post-traumatic stress disorder can be as much a set of physical problems as
psychological.

And national shortages of lifesaving drugs. Last week a group of infectious
disease physicians called for a national strategy to deal with drug shortages in
Australia. This is an under-the-radar issue with several powerful antibiotics in
short supply nationally, with some states being held hostage to higher prices
from suppliers or substitution for medications which are not so fit-for-purpose.
Someone who has documented the issue is Professor Allen Cheng in the
Department of Infectious Diseases at Alfred Health and he's in our Melbourne
studio. Welcome Allen.

Allen Cheng: Good afternoon.

Norman Swan: What drugs are we talking about here?

Allen Cheng: Look, there has been quite a range of them over the last couple of
years, so the most recent have been vancomycin and daptomycin which are
used for golden staph infections. We've had shortages of metronidazole,
acyclovir, penicillin, the hep B vaccine now, so it really is quite a range…

Norman Swan: Hep B vaccine?

Allen Cheng: Yes, I think one of the manufacturers has had a temporary stop to
supply of one of the vaccines.

Norman Swan: So just translate that for people who've never heard of these
drugs, vancomycin is one of the antibiotics of last resort for people who've got
 
serious infection, metronidazole treats fungal infections, acyclovir serious herpes
infections. These are not trivial drugs.

Allen Cheng: Exactly. And I think what it really goes to is that these are
lifesaving drugs and we really need to get them quickly when we do need them.

Norman Swan: So we've actually run out of them at times in Australia?

Allen Cheng: I think it's variable, I think some hospitals have had small
stockpiles left. So often when we've run out at our hospital we've just done a ring-
around and found a bit of a supply elsewhere. Sometimes the drug distributor
holds a little bit back and you give them a call and they will release you a bit of
stock if you beg and plead a bit. And sometimes we have run out completely and
we've just had to go to something else or to another overseas supplier.

Norman Swan: And you've done a survey of infectious disease physicians who
reckon half the time patients come to some harm or at least they don't benefit as
much as they should.

Allen Cheng: Yes, there are three major impacts on patients. The lack of
availability is really like as if the bug was resistant, you don't have that treatment
option for that infection, and sometimes that's really important. So penicillin for
syphilis is really the only treatment, all the others are second best. So when we
had problems with the penicillin supply we really had to conserve whatever
penicillin we had for syphilis specifically.

The second problem is that sometimes the options are more toxic. So
daptomycin is an example of that where when we ran out of that we had to move
to a different antibiotic called linezolid which you can't really use for more than
two weeks or it causes bone marrow toxicity and nerve damage. And then the
third problem is that sometimes we have to go to broader spectrum antibiotics.
So when we ran out of penicillin, the option for that is often ceftriaxone, that's a
broad spectrum antibiotic that can generate antibiotic resistant organisms in
itself. So that has an impact on our what we call antibiotic stewardship programs.

Norman Swan: And I've also seen some data where when you go to another
manufacturer they charge you 10 times as much. You know, where drugs that
might cost $4,000 for a course costs $40,000. It's just extraordinary.
 
Allen Cheng: Yes, so I guess there's two aspects to the cost. There's the
procurement cost, which obviously can be significant, and often there are small
manufacturers or small distributors that step in. But also the cost of just the
pharmacist having to source these.

Norman Swan: So why do these shortages occur? It's sounding like a Third
World nation.

Allen Cheng: I would probably emphasise that this is a little bit of a First World
problem. So in a Third World countries they really don't have these drugs at all,
and that's a major problem…

Norman Swan: Fair enough, but why have we got a problem?

Allen Cheng: I'm not really sure. I think the main reason is that there are not
many suppliers, and particularly for antibiotics that have been generic for a long
time, manufacturers don't make a lot of profit from them, they may not invest in
state-of-the-art factories, and so if a factory goes down that can have ripple
effects. I think it also speaks to that we have really long supply chains now. So
one manufacturer will get it from another manufacturer who will get it from
somewhere else, and then there may not be very good communication up the
chain when there is a problem at a factory.

Norman Swan: And 50% of the time it's a quality issue and the factory is taken
off-line and suddenly you discover you're not getting the drug anymore.

Allen Cheng: Yes, exactly, and even where there might be an alternative
manufacturer, they can't ramp up production very quickly, so there's still a
shortage.

Norman Swan: And it's not just antibiotics; chemotherapy, painkillers, other
things as well.

Allen Cheng: Yes, absolutely, so there's a category of lifesaving drugs, so
infrequently used vaccines, BCG for example.

Norman Swan: So when I last covered this I was told, 'There, there, sonny, don't
you worry about it, the Therapeutic goods Administration has got this in hand,
 
there's not much evidence of drug shortages in Australia.' Well, what you're
telling me is that's not true.

Allen Cheng: Yes, there are some provisions under the Therapeutic Goods Act
to ensure continued supply, but on paper they look good but they don't give us
the access when we really need them, and for antibiotics, you know, you've got
the patient in front of you, you need to treat them in hours if not minutes.

Norman Swan: So what do we need to do?

Allen Cheng: So I think we really need to recognise that these are lifesaving
drugs and that we need to build them into the hospital procurement contracts to
say that we need at least warning and if not continued supply. I think we need a
list of what are these drugs and we need to be held communicate between
hospitals to say this hospital is holding some or these hospitals can be
designated to hold a stockpile.

Norman Swan: I saw a graph of yours of Melbourne hospitals and there's quite a
lot, they've only got 7 to 10 days' supply.

Allen Cheng: Yes, so if you put the request out to a distributor often it takes 7 to
10 days to get a drug in, and when we did that survey of Melbourne hospitals we
realised that we were all holding the same drug, and some of the drugs that we
really did want, none of the hospitals were holding.

Norman Swan: Terrifying. And I assume this is not just a Victorian problem?

Allen Cheng: No, it would be certainly a national problem.

Norman Swan: So we need action.

Allen Cheng: We do, and I think it just needs to be coordinated so that we are all
on the same page and can do it most efficiently.

Norman Swan: Mildly scary. Allen, thanks for joining us.

Allen Cheng: No worries, thank you very much.
 
Norman Swan: Professor Allen Cheng is in the Department of Infectious
Diseases at Alfred health and he's also in the School of Public Health and
Preventative Medicine at Monash University.

You're listening to the Health Report here on RN, ABC News radio and CBC
radio across Canada. I'm Norman Swan.

Now, what could be a more purely psychological problem than post-traumatic
stress disorder where a proportion of people who have experienced traumatic
events are left with disabling anxiety, flashbacks, depression, behavioural issues,
and sometimes drug and alcohol use. PTSD can affect up to 20% of Australian
military personnel who have seen active duty, but it also occurs to non-military
personnel after traumatic events. Well, a study in today's edition of the Medical
Journal of Australia has findings which suggests that PTSD is not just a
psychological condition. The study concludes that PTSD affects the whole body
and should be considered what's called a systemic disorder, like diabetes for
example, which involves multiple organs. And it could help to explain why PTSD
has been so hard to treat.

Professor Darrell Crawford is director of research at the Gallipoli Medical
Research Foundation at the University of Queensland, and he's in our Brisbane
studio. Welcome to the Health Report.

Darrell Crawford: Good afternoon Norman.

Norman Swan: So tell us about this study that you did.

Darrell Crawford: Well, this is a very rigorous study of the nature and
prevalence of physical comorbidities in patients with PTSD.

Norman Swan: And when you say comorbidities, these are problems which
coincide or go along with the other condition, in this case it's PTSD.

Darrell Crawford: That's correct, and they were determined by a self-reporting
questionnaire that our subjects completed, as well as a battery of advanced non-
invasive diagnostic tests that help us to define the extent and nature of these
problems.

Norman Swan: And these were Vietnam veterans?
 
Darrell Crawford: These are Vietnam veterans, that's correct, yes.

Norman Swan: So they're not young anymore.

Darrell Crawford: No, they're not, and, as you know, these are veterans with
trauma exposure almost 50 years ago, so I think that is one of the interesting
things here, that these symptoms and the health effects of this trauma exposure
continues for decades after the initial exposure.

Norman Swan: So you compared them to people who had experienced trauma
but didn't have PTSD, and you were looking at the differences between the two
groups.

Darrell Crawford: Yes, so we had 105 patients who were confirmed by a series
of tests to have PTSD, and 106 who were negative. So we had quite a large
sample size, and we investigated these patients, as I said, with a variety of
diagnostic tests and self-reporting questionnaires.

Norman Swan: So what did you find?

Darrell Crawford: We found some interesting facts. I guess the highlight facts
are that the patients with PTSD had a four times higher risk of previous acute
myocardial infarction.

Norman Swan: Heart attack.

Darrell Crawford: Heart attack. And they had about a twofold increase in sleep
disturbances and particularly obstructive sleep apnoea and restless legs. A
twofold increase in peptic ulcer disease and irritable bowel syndrome and
constipation. There were a number of lifestyle factors I think that contributed to
diseases that are really coping responses. And so, for instance, we found that
the patients with PTSD had slightly higher body mass indexes, they consumed
more cigarettes and had a higher lifetime alcohol consumption. Clearly these sort
of factors impacted on some of the adverse outcomes of some of the diagnostic
tests that we employed.

Norman Swan: But you removed those factors as well. You subtracted those
factors from it and you still found physical symptoms and indeed serious
 
outcomes independent of the fact that they smoked and maybe ate too much
unhealthy food.

Darrell Crawford: Yes, I think this is actually a real strength of the study, was
trying to tease out those factors which were related to lifestyle factors or to
depression and anxiety, which are obviously often part and parcel of the PTSD
complex. We were left with some health outcomes that were unexplained by
either lifestyle factors or by anxiety or depression.

Norman Swan: And were they particular or was it just part of that general
grouping of heart disease and…?

Darrell Crawford: No, they were quite particular, such as peptic ulcer disease,
irritable bowel syndrome, constipation, hearing loss, and then some changes in
respiratory measurements as well as some biochemical tests.

Norman Swan: So you're making a call here that this should be called a
systemic disorder, in other words a disorder that affects the whole body, not just
the mind. But of course we've got a situation here where we've grown up with this
Cartesian…you know, Descartes said the mind and the body were split, but in
fact the mind and body are one. Are we talking about a complex interaction
between what goes on in the brain and the rest of the body? How do you explain
what's going on? Because it's not just a secondary phenomenon to stress and
lifestyle problems as a result.

Darrell Crawford: Yes, I think that we have to regard this as a condition which
has a number of physical comorbidities that in their own right affect these
patients' overall health. And the outcomes which remain unexplained by the
process of this study, there still are potential explanations that are not related to
chemical transmission or other factors or stress responses.

Norman Swan: What do you mean?

Darrell Crawford: Well, I think if you look at, say, peptic ulcer disease, it's
possible that there may have been for some reason or another a higher exposure
to Helicobacter in those patients with PTSD.
 
Norman Swan: And I think there's a research project that has gone on looking at
more recent Middle Eastern campaigns which suggest the more desert
environment, the more dirty the environment that you've been exposed to, the
more physical problems you've got along with your PTSD.

Darrell Crawford: Yes, so I think we do have to try to tease out some of these
factors. But I think that there is an increasing shift towards the idea, as you say,
of trying to link physical symptoms, which we all feel in times of stress with
central neurological…

Norman Swan: So does the feedback loop go the other way, that the physical
symptoms make a psychological problem worse?

Darrell Crawford: I think it probably does. I think that these factors that we've
identified would continue to impact adversely on the health of the veterans with
PTSD.

Norman Swan: So what does it mean for treatment? Because it is not just
veterans we're talking about here.

Darrell Crawford: I know, and I think that it's not just Vietnam veterans either. I
think that…to me I think that the pointy end of this really is that we have to
continue to address the health risk behaviours in Vietnam veterans and also in
younger veterans. I think it is reasonable to assume that if we neglect our
younger veterans, that the same health outcomes that we've seen in the Vietnam
veterans will apply to the younger veterans. I think that it should alert healthcare
providers to the underlying diagnosis of PTSD when patients with a history of
trauma exposure present with this sort of cluster of physical symptoms.

Norman Swan: So keep your eyes open and your attitudes in a box and look at
the whole person.

Darrell Crawford: Yes, I think so.

Norman Swan: Thank you very much Darrell for coming on the program.

Darrell Crawford: Thank you very much.
 
Norman Swan: Darrell Crawford is director of research at the Gallipoli Medical
Research Foundation at the University of Queensland.

Many men when they have a PSA blood test to see if they may be at higher risk
of prostate cancer are sent off for a prostate biopsy. Most of them will have the
biopsy performed through the rectum. A leading Melbourne urologist argues that
a transrectal prostate biopsy in the modern era is barbaric, dangerous and
irresponsible. And this same urologist has evidence of a better way to do the
procedure. He is associate Professor Jeremy Grummet at Alfred Health and
Monash University.

Strong words Jeremy!

Jeremy Grummet: Yes, hi Norman, I really just used those words to catch your
attention.

Norman Swan: Well, you've got it!

Jeremy Grummet: That's good. I suppose when you know that there is an
alternative available that's safer, it does shift your perspective a fair bit on how
the traditional…

Norman Swan: So what's the safety issue?

Jeremy Grummet: Okay, so normally as you mentioned when you do a prostate
biopsy you are going through the rectum. The safety issue therefore is that you
are passing biopsy needles through the rectal wall, and of course the rectum's
whole job is to store faeces. So it makes it extremely difficult not to introduce
bacteria into the prostate, and the prostate is normally a sterile organ with a very
good blood supply. So the problem with that of course is that you can then create
a severe infection which is otherwise known as septicaemia or infection in the
bloodstream.

We try and counter that with some fairly high-powered broad-spectrum antibiotics
prophylactically, but what we are finding around the world is that those same
antibiotics are starting to lose their effect, and the reason for that is that the
normal rectal flora, which is the normal rectal bacteria in people going about their
 
daily business which are not causing any problems are becoming more resistant
as time goes on to the usual antibiotics that we use.

Norman Swan: So we've got a combination of introducing these organisms and
the antibiotic cover that you give being less effective or not effective at all.

Jeremy Grummet: Correct. And so you can avoid the entire issue by simply
passing the biopsy needles through the skin instead of through the rectum, so
you are not dealing with rectal flora at all, you're just dealing with what we call
skin commensals which are the normal bacteria, the good bacteria that live on
the skin, and they are very easy to get rid of just by typical surgical preparation
with either betadine or chlorhexidine, just typical disinfectants.

Norman Swan: So where is this skin, Jeremy? As I cross my legs again!

Jeremy Grummet: It's a very sensitive part of the body, it's the perineum. So in
men it's between the scrotum and the anus. And it might sound like not the
cleanest part of your body but in fact it is really no different, particularly once the
betadine swabs have been over it, to any other part of the skin.

Norman Swan: So rusted-on urologists who love doing the transrectal biopsy
say it's terrific, you can feel it and you can get to all different parts of the prostate
and you can do an MRI scan which really makes it more accurate, whereas it's a
pig in a poke, so to speak, when you're doing it transperineally.

Jeremy Grummet: No, I don't think that's true actually. I would argue the
opposite. I think the transperineal biopsy enables you to be very accurate with
your MRI targeting. That's a whole other issue in terms of the use of MRI prior to
biopsy to increase accuracy. But when you do it via the perineum you tend to use
it with a stabilising device which enables you to perform very accurate biopsies
and you can direct your needles exactly where you want them to go. So accuracy
is not an issue at all.

Norman Swan: So you pick up the tissue if it's going to be there.

Jeremy Grummet: Yes, you almost always do, and you certainly do…the other
thing is of course because you're going through the skin you can really take
 
many more biopsies if you feel that is necessary, then what you might be
comfortable with going through the rectum.

Norman Swan: So you've got a series now I think of 1,500 patients where you've
done transperineal biopsies.

Jeremy Grummet: Well, we've certainly published on nearly 1,200 consecutive
transperineal biopsies, and we've got a rate of sepsis of zero. And the really
important point about this, in addition to that…I mean, obviously we are providing
safe care for our patients in that regard, but on top of that, the last 60% of that
cohort only required a single shot of a very basic antibiotic called cefazolin, which
is a first generation cephalosporin, and what that means is it's just your standard
basic antibiotic, it's not a big-gun antibiotic. And so the point about that is that we
are also avoiding promotion of resistant bacteria by not using…

Norman Swan: You're telling me that you've got a greater incidence of resistant
bacteria, how are you getting away with a basic antibiotic?

Jeremy Grummet: Because we are not going through the rectum. So rectal flora
becomes a nonissue completely, we're just going through the skin. And I want to
point out that this is a good news story in Australia because this isn't just our
group that is performing transperineal biopsies by any means, this is right across
the country and into New Zealand as well. We did a recent survey of urologists
across both countries and we found…in fact we did the survey twice, we did it in
2012 and then again last year, and we found that the rate of urologists doing
transperineal biopsy went from one-third to two-thirds. So Australia is really
leading the world in this area, in prostate cancer diagnosis.

Norman Swan: So it's likely that your favourite urologist is doing this technique.
Does it take a while to learn how to do it?

Jeremy Grummet: Yes, it does, but not really any longer than how to learn how
to do a transrectal biopsy, which we all learnt to do as trainees. So I think one of
the great limiting steps has been having access to the equipment. And so still
there are centres out there which don't have access to the equipment. And the
other issue that is a real issue and certainly faced in particular overseas is that
when you do a transperineal biopsy, the vast majority of the time you are doing it
 
under a general anaesthetic, and that means you've got to take up operating
theatre time.

Norman Swan: So the cost is higher.

Jeremy Grummet: Well, that's right, there's going to be a higher cost. However,
if you then compare that to the cost of avoiding sepsis…and sepsis sometimes
involves admissions to the intensive care unit…

Norman Swan: I think you found that it cost $4 million over five years at the
Alfred.

Jeremy Grummet: Yes, it's high. And so if you can avoid that cost of sepsis, well
then you may well be saving money and also saving lives.

Norman Swan: So there you are, uncross your legs and ask for a
transperineal biopsy if you need it. Jeremy, thanks very much for joining us.

Jeremy Grummet: No worries Norman, thank you.

Norman Swan: Jeremy Grummet of Alfred Health, and I've included links to a
number of Jeremy's research papers on the Health Report's website.

In the history of extraordinary trauma since first contact, probably the most
traumatic for Australian Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people has been
what's called the stolen generations where Aboriginal children were forcibly and
sometimes brutally taken from their families. Canada has also had its stolen
generations through residential schools. What's different about Canada is that
they had a Truth and Reconciliation Commission to confront that past and which
made recommendations in a variety of areas, including health. Dr Nel Wieman
was Canada's first female aboriginal psychiatrist and is based at the McMaster
University in Ontario. And Nel is working to implement some of these calls to
action from the Commission. Nel is in Melbourne for the Leaders in Indigenous
Medical Education conference. Welcome to the Health Report.

Nel Wieman: Thank you Norman, it's wonderful to be here.

Norman Swan: And you're going out in Canada through CBC radio, I think it
goes to air at some ungodly hour like 4:30 in the morning.
 
Nel Wieman: It's terrific.

Norman Swan: So Nel, just briefly tell us what these calls to actions where in the
health area in Canada from this stolen generation, although you don't call it that
in Canada.

Nel Wieman: Right. So when the Truth and Reconciliation finally finished its
seven-year process they came out with 94 separate calls to action that were
grouped into various themes. And the health group includes seven specific calls
to action. But the basic themes amongst those seven are, for example,
increasing the number of indigenous health professionals to work with our own
people, and that would be health professionals in a variety of disciplines including
medicine, nursing, occupational therapy et cetera.

The second theme was centred around the recognition of the value of traditional
healing practices, and making those practices available to indigenous people as
part of accessing healthcare in general. And the third theme centred around
academic institutions like universities, places that train health professionals, not
just indigenous health professionals but all health professionals, that they receive
mandatory training as part of integrated into the curriculum that they receive
during their education on indigenous issues in general, the history of indigenous
people in Canada, and specific issues around indigenous health and social
determinants and cultural determinants of health.

Norman Swan: When global issues around indigenous peoples, First Nations as
you call them in Canada, are discussed, it's always said that the Australian
Aboriginal people are in the worst situation, New Zealand Maori are better off,
and Canadian First Nations are better off, both of which because they have
treaties and are better recognised by their countries. But reading through some
of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, it's not a great story.

Nel Wieman: No, it's not a great story. The process that we went through with
the TRC in Canada was very important, and I think one of the things that really
needs to happen, not just in the health sphere and those of us who work with
indigenous people in health contexts, but for the general Canadian population
and the world to realise that this process happened and why it is happening. I
think if you ask the average Canadian on the street, they may not even know that
 
we actually went through a process of speaking our truth and coming up with
these calls to action. So that's one thing that Canada can do a lot better at. The
academic institutions on the other hand I think are feeling a bit of pressure now to
act upon these calls, and that's why I think there's been a lot of more attention
paid to it over the last year or so.

Norman Swan: So what's happening at McMaster, which is known as a frontline
more innovative medical school than some of the others in Canada.

Nel Wieman: Right. So McMaster University has a reputation for social
responsibility, social accountability. But in terms of…for example, if we look at the
calls to action around curriculum, that's something that we've just started to
address. So in fact the trainees at McMaster University in, for example, the
medical school, receive actually very little exposure to indigenous health issues
at present. But we are hoping to increase that now that we have the momentum
of the Truth and Reconciliation behind us.

Norman Swan: So this is things like cultural awareness training and so on.

Nel Wieman: Yes. For example…McMaster University…I mean, every medical
school now in Canada admits a very diverse class. So some of the students may
not be even that aware of indigenous health issues, and that's why it's important
to include it as part of the regular curriculum and not just offer it, say, on an
elective basis.

Norman Swan: And are there quotas for First Nation candidates?

Nel Wieman: No, it really varies from school to school, but at McMaster
University we have what's called a facilitated admissions process. So if someone
meets the basic academic standards that all students have to meet, then the
program that I work in which is the Indigenous Students Health Sciences
Program, we are able to provide support to those students as they go through the
admissions process, and we can recommend whether they are offered admission
to the medical school or not. But it has to be very clear to all the students that
everyone starts at the same point, they meet the same academic criteria that any
other student has to meet.

Norman Swan: So nothing patronising.
 
Nel Wieman: Yes.

Norman Swan: And just finally, the assumption is when you don't think about it
too hard as well, an Aboriginal kid will come into medical school in Australia and
they will go and work in an Aboriginal medical service, but why shouldn't they,
like you, become a psychiatrist or an obstetrician or what have you, it's just
having more indigenous people in the healthcare system in general. Do you
share that attitude?

Nel Wieman: Yes, I do actually. I think for myself as one of the first aboriginal
psychiatrists in Canada, is mental health issues are actually very predominant on
the needs of indigenous people in my country and as well as Australia I imagine.
But I really do think it's important as an indigenous physician that we should be
able to work wherever we want to across the country, bearing in mind that
indigenous people live in all sorts of settings across the country. We are not just
confined to small remote communities in the North. In fact more than half of
indigenous people in Canada live in urban centres.

Norman Swan: Nel, thank you very much for joining us.

Nel Wieman: Thank you very much for having me, and it's a pleasure to visit
Australia.

Norman Swan: Nel Wieman works at McMaster University in Hamilton, Ontario.

I'm Norman Swan and this has been the Health Report. See you next time.

Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swan. Today, important consumer advice for men heading for a prostate
biopsy. Barbaric is what one urologist calls the commonest technique for doing
this. Keep your legs crossed till then.

Canada's first female aboriginal psychiatrist is on the program, Canadian First
Nations, like ours, experienced stolen generations, in their case through
residential schools. But unlike Australia, Canada has had a Truth and
Reconciliation Commission. Find out more later.

How post-traumatic stress disorder can be as much a set of physical problems as
psychological.

And national shortages of lifesaving drugs. Last week a group of infectious
disease physicians called for a national strategy to deal with drug shortages in
Australia. This is an under-the-radar issue with several powerful antibiotics in
short supply nationally, with some states being held hostage to higher prices
from suppliers or substitution for medications which are not so fit-for-purpose.
Someone who has documented the issue is Professor Allen Cheng in the
Department of Infectious Diseases at Alfred Health and he's in our Melbourne
studio. Welcome Allen.

Allen Cheng: Good afternoon.

Norman Swan: What drugs are we talking about here?

Allen Cheng: Look, there has been quite a range of them over the last couple of
years, so the most recent have been vancomycin and daptomycin which are
used for golden staph infections. We've had shortages of metronidazole,
acyclovir, penicillin, the hep B vaccine now, so it really is quite a range…

Norman Swan: Hep B vaccine?

Allen Cheng: Yes, I think one of the manufacturers has had a temporary stop to
supply of one of the vaccines.

Norman Swan: So just translate that for people who've never heard of these
drugs, vancomycin is one of the antibiotics of last resort for people who've got

serious infection, metronidazole treats fungal infections, acyclovir serious herpes
infections. These are not trivial drugs.

Allen Cheng: Exactly. And I think what it really goes to is that these are
lifesaving drugs and we really need to get them quickly when we do need them.

Norman Swan: So we've actually run out of them at times in Australia?

Allen Cheng: I think it's variable, I think some hospitals have had small
stockpiles left. So often when we've run out at our hospital we've just done a ring-
around and found a bit of a supply elsewhere. Sometimes the drug distributor
holds a little bit back and you give them a call and they will release you a bit of
stock if you beg and plead a bit. And sometimes we have run out completely and
we've just had to go to something else or to another overseas supplier.

Norman Swan: And you've done a survey of infectious disease physicians who
reckon half the time patients come to some harm or at least they don't benefit as
much as they should.

Allen Cheng: Yes, there are three major impacts on patients. The lack of
availability is really like as if the bug was resistant, you don't have that treatment
option for that infection, and sometimes that's really important. So penicillin for
syphilis is really the only treatment, all the others are second best. So when we
had problems with the penicillin supply we really had to conserve whatever
penicillin we had for syphilis specifically.

The second problem is that sometimes the options are more toxic. So
daptomycin is an example of that where when we ran out of that we had to move
to a different antibiotic called linezolid which you can't really use for more than
two weeks or it causes bone marrow toxicity and nerve damage. And then the
third problem is that sometimes we have to go to broader spectrum antibiotics.
So when we ran out of penicillin, the option for that is often ceftriaxone, that's a
broad spectrum antibiotic that can generate antibiotic resistant organisms in
itself. So that has an impact on our what we call antibiotic stewardship programs.

Norman Swan: And I've also seen some data where when you go to another
manufacturer they charge you 10 times as much. You know, where drugs that
might cost $4,000 for a course costs $40,000. It's just extraordinary.

Allen Cheng: Yes, so I guess there's two aspects to the cost. There's the
procurement cost, which obviously can be significant, and often there are small
manufacturers or small distributors that step in. But also the cost of just the
pharmacist having to source these.

Norman Swan: So why do these shortages occur? It's sounding like a Third
World nation.

Allen Cheng: I would probably emphasise that this is a little bit of a First World
problem. So in a Third World countries they really don't have these drugs at all,
and that's a major problem…

Norman Swan: Fair enough, but why have we got a problem?

Allen Cheng: I'm not really sure. I think the main reason is that there are not
many suppliers, and particularly for antibiotics that have been generic for a long
time, manufacturers don't make a lot of profit from them, they may not invest in
state-of-the-art factories, and so if a factory goes down that can have ripple
effects. I think it also speaks to that we have really long supply chains now. So
one manufacturer will get it from another manufacturer who will get it from
somewhere else, and then there may not be very good communication up the
chain when there is a problem at a factory.

Norman Swan: And 50% of the time it's a quality issue and the factory is taken
off-line and suddenly you discover you're not getting the drug anymore.

Allen Cheng: Yes, exactly, and even where there might be an alternative
manufacturer, they can't ramp up production very quickly, so there's still a
shortage.

Norman Swan: And it's not just antibiotics; chemotherapy, painkillers, other
things as well.

Allen Cheng: Yes, absolutely, so there's a category of lifesaving drugs, so
infrequently used vaccines, BCG for example.

Norman Swan: So when I last covered this I was told, 'There, there, sonny, don't
you worry about it, the Therapeutic goods Administration has got this in hand,

there's not much evidence of drug shortages in Australia.' Well, what you're
telling me is that's not true.

Allen Cheng: Yes, there are some provisions under the Therapeutic Goods Act
to ensure continued supply, but on paper they look good but they don't give us
the access when we really need them, and for antibiotics, you know, you've got
the patient in front of you, you need to treat them in hours if not minutes.

Norman Swan: So what do we need to do?

Allen Cheng: So I think we really need to recognise that these are lifesaving
drugs and that we need to build them into the hospital procurement contracts to
say that we need at least warning and if not continued supply. I think we need a
list of what are these drugs and we need to be held communicate between
hospitals to say this hospital is holding some or these hospitals can be
designated to hold a stockpile.

Norman Swan: I saw a graph of yours of Melbourne hospitals and there's quite a
lot, they've only got 7 to 10 days' supply.

Allen Cheng: Yes, so if you put the request out to a distributor often it takes 7 to
10 days to get a drug in, and when we did that survey of Melbourne hospitals we
realised that we were all holding the same drug, and some of the drugs that we
really did want, none of the hospitals were holding.

Norman Swan: Terrifying. And I assume this is not just a Victorian problem?

Allen Cheng: No, it would be certainly a national problem.

Norman Swan: So we need action.

Allen Cheng: We do, and I think it just needs to be coordinated so that we are all
on the same page and can do it most efficiently.

Norman Swan: Mildly scary. Allen, thanks for joining us.

Allen Cheng: No worries, thank you very much.

Norman Swan: Professor Allen Cheng is in the Department of Infectious
Diseases at Alfred health and he's also in the School of Public Health and
Preventative Medicine at Monash University.

You're listening to the Health Report here on RN, ABC News radio and CBC
radio across Canada. I'm Norman Swan.

Now, what could be a more purely psychological problem than post-traumatic
stress disorder where a proportion of people who have experienced traumatic
events are left with disabling anxiety, flashbacks, depression, behavioural issues,
and sometimes drug and alcohol use. PTSD can affect up to 20% of Australian
military personnel who have seen active duty, but it also occurs to non-military
personnel after traumatic events. Well, a study in today's edition of the Medical
Journal of Australia has findings which suggests that PTSD is not just a
psychological condition. The study concludes that PTSD affects the whole body
and should be considered what's called a systemic disorder, like diabetes for
example, which involves multiple organs. And it could help to explain why PTSD
has been so hard to treat.

Professor Darrell Crawford is director of research at the Gallipoli Medical
Research Foundation at the University of Queensland, and he's in our Brisbane
studio. Welcome to the Health Report.

Darrell Crawford: Good afternoon Norman.

Norman Swan: So tell us about this study that you did.

Darrell Crawford: Well, this is a very rigorous study of the nature and
prevalence of physical comorbidities in patients with PTSD.

Norman Swan: And when you say comorbidities, these are problems which
coincide or go along with the other condition, in this case it's PTSD.

Darrell Crawford: That's correct, and they were determined by a self-reporting
questionnaire that our subjects completed, as well as a battery of advanced non-
invasive diagnostic tests that help us to define the extent and nature of these
problems.

Norman Swan: And these were Vietnam veterans?

Darrell Crawford: These are Vietnam veterans, that's correct, yes.

Norman Swan: So they're not young anymore.

Darrell Crawford: No, they're not, and, as you know, these are veterans with
trauma exposure almost 50 years ago, so I think that is one of the interesting
things here, that these symptoms and the health effects of this trauma exposure
continues for decades after the initial exposure.

Norman Swan: So you compared them to people who had experienced trauma
but didn't have PTSD, and you were looking at the differences between the two
groups.

Darrell Crawford: Yes, so we had 105 patients who were confirmed by a series
of tests to have PTSD, and 106 who were negative. So we had quite a large
sample size, and we investigated these patients, as I said, with a variety of
diagnostic tests and self-reporting questionnaires.

Norman Swan: So what did you find?

Darrell Crawford: We found some interesting facts. I guess the highlight facts
are that the patients with PTSD had a four times higher risk of previous acute
myocardial infarction.

Norman Swan: Heart attack.

Darrell Crawford: Heart attack. And they had about a twofold increase in sleep
disturbances and particularly obstructive sleep apnoea and restless legs. A
twofold increase in peptic ulcer disease and irritable bowel syndrome and
constipation. There were a number of lifestyle factors I think that contributed to
diseases that are really coping responses. And so, for instance, we found that
the patients with PTSD had slightly higher body mass indexes, they consumed
more cigarettes and had a higher lifetime alcohol consumption. Clearly these sort
of factors impacted on some of the adverse outcomes of some of the diagnostic
tests that we employed.

Norman Swan: But you removed those factors as well. You subtracted those
factors from it and you still found physical symptoms and indeed serious

outcomes independent of the fact that they smoked and maybe ate too much
unhealthy food.

Darrell Crawford: Yes, I think this is actually a real strength of the study, was
trying to tease out those factors which were related to lifestyle factors or to
depression and anxiety, which are obviously often part and parcel of the PTSD
complex. We were left with some health outcomes that were unexplained by
either lifestyle factors or by anxiety or depression.

Norman Swan: And were they particular or was it just part of that general
grouping of heart disease and…?

Darrell Crawford: No, they were quite particular, such as peptic ulcer disease,
irritable bowel syndrome, constipation, hearing loss, and then some changes in
respiratory measurements as well as some biochemical tests.

Norman Swan: So you're making a call here that this should be called a
systemic disorder, in other words a disorder that affects the whole body, not just
the mind. But of course we've got a situation here where we've grown up with this
Cartesian…you know, Descartes said the mind and the body were split, but in
fact the mind and body are one. Are we talking about a complex interaction
between what goes on in the brain and the rest of the body? How do you explain
what's going on? Because it's not just a secondary phenomenon to stress and
lifestyle problems as a result.

Darrell Crawford: Yes, I think that we have to regard this as a condition which
has a number of physical comorbidities that in their own right affect these
patients' overall health. And the outcomes which remain unexplained by the
process of this study, there still are potential explanations that are not related to
chemical transmission or other factors or stress responses.

Norman Swan: What do you mean?

Darrell Crawford: Well, I think if you look at, say, peptic ulcer disease, it's
possible that there may have been for some reason or another a higher exposure
to Helicobacter in those patients with PTSD.

Norman Swan: And I think there's a research project that has gone on looking at
more recent Middle Eastern campaigns which suggest the more desert
environment, the more dirty the environment that you've been exposed to, the
more physical problems you've got along with your PTSD.

Darrell Crawford: Yes, so I think we do have to try to tease out some of these
factors. But I think that there is an increasing shift towards the idea, as you say,
of trying to link physical symptoms, which we all feel in times of stress with
central neurological…

Norman Swan: So does the feedback loop go the other way, that the physical
symptoms make a psychological problem worse?

Darrell Crawford: I think it probably does. I think that these factors that we've
identified would continue to impact adversely on the health of the veterans with
PTSD.

Norman Swan: So what does it mean for treatment? Because it is not just
veterans we're talking about here.

Darrell Crawford: I know, and I think that it's not just Vietnam veterans either. I
think that…to me I think that the pointy end of this really is that we have to
continue to address the health risk behaviours in Vietnam veterans and also in
younger veterans. I think it is reasonable to assume that if we neglect our
younger veterans, that the same health outcomes that we've seen in the Vietnam
veterans will apply to the younger veterans. I think that it should alert healthcare
providers to the underlying diagnosis of PTSD when patients with a history of
trauma exposure present with this sort of cluster of physical symptoms.

Norman Swan: So keep your eyes open and your attitudes in a box and look at
the whole person.

Darrell Crawford: Yes, I think so.

Norman Swan: Thank you very much Darrell for coming on the program.

Darrell Crawford: Thank you very much.

Norman Swan: Darrell Crawford is director of research at the Gallipoli Medical
Research Foundation at the University of Queensland.

Many men when they have a PSA blood test to see if they may be at higher risk
of prostate cancer are sent off for a prostate biopsy. Most of them will have the
biopsy performed through the rectum. A leading Melbourne urologist argues that
a transrectal prostate biopsy in the modern era is barbaric, dangerous and
irresponsible. And this same urologist has evidence of a better way to do the
procedure. He is associate Professor Jeremy Grummet at Alfred Health and
Monash University.

Strong words Jeremy!

Jeremy Grummet: Yes, hi Norman, I really just used those words to catch your
attention.

Norman Swan: Well, you've got it!

Jeremy Grummet: That's good. I suppose when you know that there is an
alternative available that's safer, it does shift your perspective a fair bit on how
the traditional…

Norman Swan: So what's the safety issue?

Jeremy Grummet: Okay, so normally as you mentioned when you do a prostate
biopsy you are going through the rectum. The safety issue therefore is that you
are passing biopsy needles through the rectal wall, and of course the rectum's
whole job is to store faeces. So it makes it extremely difficult not to introduce
bacteria into the prostate, and the prostate is normally a sterile organ with a very
good blood supply. So the problem with that of course is that you can then create
a severe infection which is otherwise known as septicaemia or infection in the
bloodstream.

We try and counter that with some fairly high-powered broad-spectrum antibiotics
prophylactically, but what we are finding around the world is that those same
antibiotics are starting to lose their effect, and the reason for that is that the
normal rectal flora, which is the normal rectal bacteria in people going about their

daily business which are not causing any problems are becoming more resistant
as time goes on to the usual antibiotics that we use.

Norman Swan: So we've got a combination of introducing these organisms and
the antibiotic cover that you give being less effective or not effective at all.

Jeremy Grummet: Correct. And so you can avoid the entire issue by simply
passing the biopsy needles through the skin instead of through the rectum, so
you are not dealing with rectal flora at all, you're just dealing with what we call
skin commensals which are the normal bacteria, the good bacteria that live on
the skin, and they are very easy to get rid of just by typical surgical preparation
with either betadine or chlorhexidine, just typical disinfectants.

Norman Swan: So where is this skin, Jeremy? As I cross my legs again!

Jeremy Grummet: It's a very sensitive part of the body, it's the perineum. So in
men it's between the scrotum and the anus. And it might sound like not the
cleanest part of your body but in fact it is really no different, particularly once the
betadine swabs have been over it, to any other part of the skin.

Norman Swan: So rusted-on urologists who love doing the transrectal biopsy
say it's terrific, you can feel it and you can get to all different parts of the prostate
and you can do an MRI scan which really makes it more accurate, whereas it's a
pig in a poke, so to speak, when you're doing it transperineally.

Jeremy Grummet: No, I don't think that's true actually. I would argue the
opposite. I think the transperineal biopsy enables you to be very accurate with
your MRI targeting. That's a whole other issue in terms of the use of MRI prior to
biopsy to increase accuracy. But when you do it via the perineum you tend to use
it with a stabilising device which enables you to perform very accurate biopsies
and you can direct your needles exactly where you want them to go. So accuracy
is not an issue at all.

Norman Swan: So you pick up the tissue if it's going to be there.

Jeremy Grummet: Yes, you almost always do, and you certainly do…the other
thing is of course because you're going through the skin you can really take

many more biopsies if you feel that is necessary, then what you might be
comfortable with going through the rectum.

Norman Swan: So you've got a series now I think of 1,500 patients where you've
done transperineal biopsies.

Jeremy Grummet: Well, we've certainly published on nearly 1,200 consecutive
transperineal biopsies, and we've got a rate of sepsis of zero. And the really
important point about this, in addition to that…I mean, obviously we are providing
safe care for our patients in that regard, but on top of that, the last 60% of that
cohort only required a single shot of a very basic antibiotic called cefazolin, which
is a first generation cephalosporin, and what that means is it's just your standard
basic antibiotic, it's not a big-gun antibiotic. And so the point about that is that we
are also avoiding promotion of resistant bacteria by not using…

Norman Swan: You're telling me that you've got a greater incidence of resistant
bacteria, how are you getting away with a basic antibiotic?

Jeremy Grummet: Because we are not going through the rectum. So rectal flora
becomes a nonissue completely, we're just going through the skin. And I want to
point out that this is a good news story in Australia because this isn't just our
group that is performing transperineal biopsies by any means, this is right across
the country and into New Zealand as well. We did a recent survey of urologists
across both countries and we found…in fact we did the survey twice, we did it in
2012 and then again last year, and we found that the rate of urologists doing
transperineal biopsy went from one-third to two-thirds. So Australia is really
leading the world in this area, in prostate cancer diagnosis.

Norman Swan: So it's likely that your favourite urologist is doing this technique.
Does it take a while to learn how to do it?

Jeremy Grummet: Yes, it does, but not really any longer than how to learn how
to do a transrectal biopsy, which we all learnt to do as trainees. So I think one of
the great limiting steps has been having access to the equipment. And so still
there are centres out there which don't have access to the equipment. And the
other issue that is a real issue and certainly faced in particular overseas is that
when you do a transperineal biopsy, the vast majority of the time you are doing it

under a general anaesthetic, and that means you've got to take up operating
theatre time.

Norman Swan: So the cost is higher.

Jeremy Grummet: Well, that's right, there's going to be a higher cost. However,
if you then compare that to the cost of avoiding sepsis…and sepsis sometimes
involves admissions to the intensive care unit…

Norman Swan: I think you found that it cost $4 million over five years at the
Alfred.

Jeremy Grummet: Yes, it's high. And so if you can avoid that cost of sepsis, well
then you may well be saving money and also saving lives.

Norman Swan: So there you are, uncross your legs and ask for a
transperineal biopsy if you need it. Jeremy, thanks very much for joining us.

Jeremy Grummet: No worries Norman, thank you.

Norman Swan: Jeremy Grummet of Alfred Health, and I've included links to a
number of Jeremy's research papers on the Health Report's website.

In the history of extraordinary trauma since first contact, probably the most
traumatic for Australian Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people has been
what's called the stolen generations where Aboriginal children were forcibly and
sometimes brutally taken from their families. Canada has also had its stolen
generations through residential schools. What's different about Canada is that
they had a Truth and Reconciliation Commission to confront that past and which
made recommendations in a variety of areas, including health. Dr Nel Wieman
was Canada's first female aboriginal psychiatrist and is based at the McMaster
University in Ontario. And Nel is working to implement some of these calls to
action from the Commission. Nel is in Melbourne for the Leaders in Indigenous
Medical Education conference. Welcome to the Health Report.

Nel Wieman: Thank you Norman, it's wonderful to be here.

Norman Swan: And you're going out in Canada through CBC radio, I think it
goes to air at some ungodly hour like 4:30 in the morning.

Nel Wieman: It's terrific.

Norman Swan: So Nel, just briefly tell us what these calls to actions where in the
health area in Canada from this stolen generation, although you don't call it that
in Canada.

Nel Wieman: Right. So when the Truth and Reconciliation finally finished its
seven-year process they came out with 94 separate calls to action that were
grouped into various themes. And the health group includes seven specific calls
to action. But the basic themes amongst those seven are, for example,
increasing the number of indigenous health professionals to work with our own
people, and that would be health professionals in a variety of disciplines including
medicine, nursing, occupational therapy et cetera.

The second theme was centred around the recognition of the value of traditional
healing practices, and making those practices available to indigenous people as
part of accessing healthcare in general. And the third theme centred around
academic institutions like universities, places that train health professionals, not
just indigenous health professionals but all health professionals, that they receive
mandatory training as part of integrated into the curriculum that they receive
during their education on indigenous issues in general, the history of indigenous
people in Canada, and specific issues around indigenous health and social
determinants and cultural determinants of health.

Norman Swan: When global issues around indigenous peoples, First Nations as
you call them in Canada, are discussed, it's always said that the Australian
Aboriginal people are in the worst situation, New Zealand Maori are better off,
and Canadian First Nations are better off, both of which because they have
treaties and are better recognised by their countries. But reading through some
of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, it's not a great story.

Nel Wieman: No, it's not a great story. The process that we went through with
the TRC in Canada was very important, and I think one of the things that really
needs to happen, not just in the health sphere and those of us who work with
indigenous people in health contexts, but for the general Canadian population
and the world to realise that this process happened and why it is happening. I
think if you ask the average Canadian on the street, they may not even know that

we actually went through a process of speaking our truth and coming up with
these calls to action. So that's one thing that Canada can do a lot better at. The
academic institutions on the other hand I think are feeling a bit of pressure now to
act upon these calls, and that's why I think there's been a lot of more attention
paid to it over the last year or so.

Norman Swan: So what's happening at McMaster, which is known as a frontline
more innovative medical school than some of the others in Canada.

Nel Wieman: Right. So McMaster University has a reputation for social
responsibility, social accountability. But in terms of…for example, if we look at the
calls to action around curriculum, that's something that we've just started to
address. So in fact the trainees at McMaster University in, for example, the
medical school, receive actually very little exposure to indigenous health issues
at present. But we are hoping to increase that now that we have the momentum
of the Truth and Reconciliation behind us.

Norman Swan: So this is things like cultural awareness training and so on.

Nel Wieman: Yes. For example…McMaster University…I mean, every medical
school now in Canada admits a very diverse class. So some of the students may
not be even that aware of indigenous health issues, and that's why it's important
to include it as part of the regular curriculum and not just offer it, say, on an
elective basis.

Norman Swan: And are there quotas for First Nation candidates?

Nel Wieman: No, it really varies from school to school, but at McMaster
University we have what's called a facilitated admissions process. So if someone
meets the basic academic standards that all students have to meet, then the
program that I work in which is the Indigenous Students Health Sciences
Program, we are able to provide support to those students as they go through the
admissions process, and we can recommend whether they are offered admission
to the medical school or not. But it has to be very clear to all the students that
everyone starts at the same point, they meet the same academic criteria that any
other student has to meet.

Norman Swan: So nothing patronising.

Nel Wieman: Yes.

Norman Swan: And just finally, the assumption is when you don't think about it
too hard as well, an Aboriginal kid will come into medical school in Australia and
they will go and work in an Aboriginal medical service, but why shouldn't they,
like you, become a psychiatrist or an obstetrician or what have you, it's just
having more indigenous people in the healthcare system in general. Do you
share that attitude?

Nel Wieman: Yes, I do actually. I think for myself as one of the first aboriginal
psychiatrists in Canada, is mental health issues are actually very predominant on
the needs of indigenous people in my country and as well as Australia I imagine.
But I really do think it's important as an indigenous physician that we should be
able to work wherever we want to across the country, bearing in mind that
indigenous people live in all sorts of settings across the country. We are not just
confined to small remote communities in the North. In fact more than half of
indigenous people in Canada live in urban centres.

Norman Swan: Nel, thank you very much for joining us.

Nel Wieman: Thank you very much for having me, and it's a pleasure to visit
Australia.

Norman Swan: Nel Wieman works at McMaster University in Hamilton, Ontario.

I'm Norman Swan and this has been the Health Report. See you next time.
